title: Predict what an index gives
idea: Read list-and-index code and predict the single value it produces. Pure thinking practice to cement positions.

exercises.explanation: Positions: 5 at 0, 10 at 1, 15 at 2, 20 at 3. So nums[2] is 15.
Index 0 is the first value, 100. Always start your count at 0.
x at 0, y at 1, z at 2. So mix[1] gives "y", the second value.
-1 is the last value, 36. The end shortcut saves you from counting all five positions.

exercises.prompt: For vals = [11, 22, 33, 44], match each index to its value.
exercises.explanation: 0 -> 11 (first), 2 -> 33 (third), -1 -> 44 (last). Trace the position carefully each time.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

temps = [14, 17, 21]
first = temps[0]
print(first)
exercises.explanation: temps[0] is 14, and that gets stored in first. Printing first shows 14. You can save an indexed value in a variable.

exercises.prompt: The value from indexing can be stored in a variable, like  top = scores[0].
exercises.explanation: Yes. Indexing gives a single value, and any single value can go into a variable. Here top would hold the first score.

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output:

nums = [3, 6, 9]
print(nums[1])
print(nums[2])
exercises.explanation: nums[1] is 6, nums[2] is 9. Two prints, two lines, in order: 6 then 9.
-1 is 10 (last), so -2 is the one before it, 20. Negative indexes count back from the end.
All values are 7, so nums[0] is 7. Indexing gives the one value at that spot, even when the values repeat.
